strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed idea: a neural-operator-based local vector field estimator amortises ODE inference, and the paper provides a clean conceptual contrast between local (FIM-ODE) and global symbolic (ODEFormer) representations, with concrete mechanistic examples (frictionless pendulum vs CDIMA reaction) illustrating when each succeeds or fails.

Strong efficiency result: FIM-ODE (8M parameters, 0.6M pretraining systems) matches or beats ODEFormer (86M parameters, 50M systems) on ODEBench trajectory reconstruction (e.g., 84.4% vs 63.1% at sigma=0, rho=0), supporting the value of the simpler polynomial prior.

Unusually honest experimental reporting: the paper openly discloses high sensitivity to noise realisations in the low-data regime, reports 100-trial statistics (Table 7) rather than only favourable seeds, and gives a thoughtful limitations section covering the non-stationary prior, curse of dimensionality, and the fixed state dimension.

Comprehensive evaluation across regimes: ODEBench under noise/subsampling corruption, low-data OOD forecasting/imputation (VDP, FHN) against strong per-dataset baselines, real-world human motion capture, plus ablations on dataset size, discretization, number of context trajectories, vector field quality metrics, and degree-6 OOD generalisation.

Pretraining serves as an effective initialisation for finetuning: finetuned FIM-ODE yields best or near-best results on the Hegde et al. benchmarks and improves substantially on MoCap, demonstrating practical amortisation of neural ODE training at low adaptation cost.
Reproducibility appears good: full data generation, architecture, normalisation, and training details are given in Appendices B-D, and code/model release is promised.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: the architecture, loss (uncertainty weighting), corruption scheme, and finetuning procedure are largely adapted from prior FIM work (FIM-SDE, FIM-CJP, ODEFormer); the main new element is a simpler polynomial prior plus the local-representation argument. The scientific contribution is more an empirical study than a new method.

Zero-shot evidence is mixed rather than decisive. On trajectory generalisation (Table 2) FIM-ODE is only comparable to ODEFormer; in the low-data VDP/FHN tasks (Table 4) zero-shot FIM-ODE is clearly worse than both classical baselines and ODEFormer on Task 1 (0.89 vs 0.22), and the 'Selected noise' row is the best of 100 trials. The paper is transparent about this, but the headline zero-shot claim is weaker than the abstract suggests.

Zero-shot MoCap results are poor and unstable (Table 5: MSE of 655.40, 295.29, 243.87 for subjects 35/39), substantially worse than all baselines; only finetuned FIM-ODE is competitive. The PCA/memory explanation is plausible but partly post-hoc.

Vector field accuracy itself is modest: cosine similarity between predicted and true vector fields is only ~0.53 with one trajectory (Figures 16-18), and reconstruction success drops sharply with dimension (65% at d=3, R2>0.9). The paper's central object is the vector field, yet direct quality metrics receive less attention than trajectory metrics.

Evaluation scale and significance: ODEBench contains only 59 usable systems (two excluded), the R2>0.9 threshold analysis shows sensitivity of conclusions to the criterion, and no statistical significance testing accompanies the headline comparisons. Benchmark modifications (dimension-based exclusion) slightly complicate comparability with ODEFormer's published results.

The 'without requiring machine learning expertise' claim is partly undercut by the finetuning recipe, which involves neural ODE training with choices of epochs, noise injection levels, initial condition spacing, and validation-based model selection (Appendix D).

Practical scope is narrow: pretraining is restricted to d<=3 autonomous polynomial ODEs of degree <=3, and the authors acknowledge the curse of dimensionality prevents scaling the prior, limiting applicability to the higher-dimensional systems common in practice.

strengths: Clear and well-structured presentation; the paper is easy to follow, and the distinction between local (neural operator) and global (symbolic) vector field representations is well motivated.

Honest and unusually transparent reporting: the paper openly discusses failure cases (e.g., the frictionless pendulum in Figure 2), the strong sensitivity of low-data results to noise realisation (Appendix E.2, Table 7), non-identifiability of the inference problem, and a substantive Limitations section (nonstationary prior, curse of dimensionality, fixed dimensionality).

The headline efficiency result is compelling: a 13M-parameter model pretrained on 0.6M simple polynomial systems matches or beats the 86M-parameter ODEFormer on ODEBench trajectory reconstruction (Table 1), supporting the claim that a simple prior plus local representation suffices.

Thorough supplementary evaluation: dataset-size scaling (E.6), discretization and trajectory-count ablations (E.4), direct vector field quality metrics (E.5), and OOD generalization to degree-6 polynomials (E.3).
Good mechanisms-level analysis (e.g., Section 5.3 explaining the PCA information bottleneck and Mori–Zwanzig memory effects for MoCap).
weaknesses: Limited originality: the contribution is largely an application of the existing FIM framework (Berghaus et al., 2024; Seifner et al., 2025a) to ODEs. The architecture is explicitly adapted from FIM-SDE (Seifner et al., 2025a), the corruption scheme follows ODEFormer, and the prior is a straightforward sparse low-degree polynomial construction. The conceptual novelty (amortised, local vs. symbolic inference) is modest.

Questionable reporting practice in the main results: Table 4 includes 'FIM-ODE (Selected noise)', which is the best of 100 noise realisations, presented alongside baselines evaluated on the fixed benchmark dataset. Even though the variability is acknowledged in the text and Appendix E.2 (mean MSE 0.575–2.511 vs. the selected 0.02), putting a cherry-picked best seed in the main comparison table is misleading.

Zero-shot performance in the harder, real-world-oriented experiments is weak, undermining the paper's central narrative: in the low-data regime zero-shot FIM-ODE (0.89/0.40/0.33) is far behind classical baselines such as GP-DNF (0.03/0.04/0.04), and on CMU MoCap subjects 35 and 39 the zero-shot results are catastrophic (MSE 655.40 and 295.29 vs. ~7–26 for baselines). The paper instead shifts the claim to finetuned performance, which also does not consistently beat GP-DNF (e.g., subject 39 long horizon: 19.89 vs. 16.21).

The ODEBench generalisation results at the headline threshold R^2 > 0.9 (Table 2) are only comparable to ODEFormer, not better, and the qualitative conclusions flip depending on threshold choice (0.8 vs. 0.9, Tables 2 vs. 6), which weakens the generality of the 'local beats global' claim.

Reproducibility is currently unmet: the pretrained model, code, and tutorials are only 'will be released online shortly', so none of the results could be verified at review time. Additionally, two ODEBench systems with dimension > 3 are excluded, which complicates direct comparability with the ODEFormer benchmark results.

The method is hard-limited to d <= 3 with a fixed dimensionality design; for a paper billed as a foundation model, this is a significant scope restriction that the authors themselves identify, and it is the direct cause of the MoCap failures.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether a simple polynomial pretraining prior with a local (neural operator) representation can rival a much larger model pretrained on a complex prior (ODEFormer) for amortised ODE inference. The 'local vs global representation' framing is a genuinely interesting angle with new understanding value.

Strong and efficient empirical results on ODEBench trajectory reconstruction (Table 1): FIM-ODE consistently outperforms ODEFormer across all noise/subsampling settings while being ~10x smaller and pretrained on ~80x fewer systems, which is a convincing efficiency result.

Transparent and thorough experimental reporting. The paper openly discloses unfavorable results: zero-shot failures in the low-data regime (Section 5.2), sensitivity to noise seeds (100-trial analysis in Appendix E.2 with full statistics), the mechanism behind zero-shot failures on MoCap subjects 35/39 (PCA information bottleneck, memory effects), and degradation on chaotic/conservative systems like the pendulum in Figure 2.

Honest limitations section that correctly identifies the non-stationary polynomial prior, the curse of dimensionality restricting pretraining to d<=3, and the hard-coded input dimensionality, with concrete future-work plans.

Extensive ablations and supplementary experiments (dataset-size scaling with diminishing returns, discretization and trajectory-count effects, per-dimension vector field RMSE/cosine similarity, degree-6 OOD polynomials), plus detailed data generation, architecture, and finetuning protocols enabling reproduction.
weaknesses: The presentation of 'FIM-ODE (Selected noise)' in the main Table 4 is the best instance out of 100 random trials. While the authors are commendably transparent about this, presenting a best-of-100 result alongside baselines evaluated on the fixed benchmark dataset risks overstating zero-shot competitiveness in the low-data regime, where the actual zero-shot results (0.89, 0.40, 0.33) are worse than ODEFormer and far worse than classical baselines.

Zero-shot performance claims are narrower than the abstract suggests. Trajectory generalisation on ODEBench (Table 2) is only comparable to ODEFormer (no consistent winner), and on MoCap, zero-shot FIM-ODE fails catastrophically on subjects 35 and 39 (MSE 655.4 and 295.3 vs ~7-26 for baselines), succeeding only for subject 09 where the 3D projection is nearly lossless.

The finetuned results are strong but the claim that they 'outperform most baselines in essentially all cases' is slightly overstated: GP-DNF still beats finetuned FIM-ODE on subject 35 long (7.03 vs 11.73) and subject 39 long (16.21 vs 19.89) in Table 5.

The core 'local beats global' thesis is supported mainly by two anecdotal case studies (Figure 2) plus aggregate tables; a more systematic analysis correlating failure modes with functional-form mismatch would strengthen the claim. Also, the multi-trajectory ODEFormer extension (Sahin et al., 2025), which is directly relevant, is cited but not compared against.

ODEBench is small (59 systems after exclusions), so the fraction-of-systems metrics carry substantial variance; some differences (e.g., Table 2) may not be statistically meaningful, and no uncertainty estimates are given for these.

Reproducibility is currently aspirational: the abstract states code and the pretrained model 'will be released online shortly', but no repository is available at review time; the reported experimental protocol is detailed enough that this is likely fixable in revision.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated extension of the Foundation Inference Model framework to ODE vector field inference, and clearly articulates the key insight that a local neural-operator representation can outperform global symbolic representations in data-rich regions while remaining queryable for dynamical-systems analysis (equilibria, Jacobians, stability types).

Evaluation is unusually thorough and honest: the paper includes a failure case (frictionless pendulum), reports ID/OOD splits on ODEBench (Table 10) showing where the method struggles (3D systems), quantifies noise-realization sensitivity in low-data regimes (Table 4, 14), and explicitly flags that 'Finetuned 2' checkpoint selection uses the evaluation window (Appendix D.1).

The headline zero-shot results are compelling: FIM-ODE substantially outperforms ODEFormer on trajectory reconstruction (Table 1, e.g., 84.4% vs 63.1% at clean conditions) while being ~10x smaller in parameters and pretrained on ~80x fewer systems from a much simpler prior, supporting the central claim about local vs global representations.

Extensive ablations (dataset size scaling, discretization effects, number of context trajectories, vector-field quality metrics, degree-6 OOD generalization) and full architectural/training details in the appendices support reproducibility; model, code, and tutorials are released.

The limitations and impact statements are candid and substantive, including the curse of dimensionality in the polynomial prior, the fixed maximum dimension, and the risk of over-interpreting inferred vector fields.
weaknesses: The main contribution is arguably incremental: the architecture, loss, uncertainty weighting, and overall framework closely follow FIM-SDE (Seifner et al., 2025a), with the primary novelty being the adaptation to deterministic ODEs, a simple polynomial prior, and the transition-based input representation. The conceptual claims about amortization and local vs. global representations are plausible but not supported by theory or controlled experiments beyond qualitative case studies.

Performance degrades sharply with dimension: on ODEBench, 3D ID reconstruction is only 16.7% and 3D generalization is 0% (Table 10), and the headline aggregate numbers are largely driven by 1D and 2D systems. The paper acknowledges this but the abstract-level claims ('strong zero-shot performance') could obscure this important weakness for readers who do not consult the appendix.

On trajectory generalization (Table 2), FIM-ODE is only comparable to ODEFormer, not better, so the superiority claim holds mainly for reconstruction. ODEBench is also small (61 systems, some splits containing a single ODE), so differences may not be statistically meaningful; no significance analysis is provided.

In the low-data regime (Section 5.2), zero-shot FIM-ODE is clearly worse than classical baselines, and the strong finetuned results rely on a checkpoint-selection protocol that uses the held-out evaluation window (Finetuned 2, Table 4/6), which the authors themselves admit is not a fully independent test protocol. The best finetuned numbers (e.g., 0.028 on VDP T1) thus risk overstating practical performance.

The claim that finetuning 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines without requiring machine learning expertise' is somewhat weakened by the fact that finetuning involves nontrivial choices (shooting method, solver, learning rates, noise injection) documented across Appendix D, and by the ambiguous framing of fairness versus baselines trained from scratch.

The pretraining prior (degree ≤ 3 polynomials, d ≤ 3, non-stationary scaling) is restrictive and the paper's own analysis (Appendix B.4) shows a systematic spatial bias in vector-field sampling near bounding-box boundaries; the consequences for out-of-support behavior of the inferred fields are not fully explored.

strengths: The paper extends the Foundation Inference Model framework to ODEs with a clean, well-motivated design: a simple polynomial prior, a transition-based transformer neural-operator that estimates the vector field locally, and uncertainty-weighted training. The 'local vs. global representation' framing versus ODEFormer is a genuinely interesting lens.

Experiments cover multiple regimes (ODEBench zero-shot, low-data forecasting/imputation, real-world motion capture) with reasonable baselines, and the paper separates in-distribution from out-of-distribution systems (Table 10), which strengthens the empirical analysis.

The interpretability analysis (fixed points, Jacobians, stability classification in Table 13 and Figure 2) is a valuable contribution: it shows neural vector fields can be queried like symbolic ones and exposes failure modes invisible to trajectory error alone.

The limitations and future-work discussion is honest and specific (non-stationary prior scaling, fixed dimensionality, curse of dimensionality), and an impact statement addresses over-interpretation risks. Code, model, and tutorials are released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental: the architecture, loss, and pretraining recipe are directly adapted from FIM-SDE (Seifner et al., 2025a), and the novelty amounts to a simple polynomial prior applied to ODEs. Given this lineage, the technical novelty is modest.

The headline claim of 'strong zero-shot performance, matching and often improving upon ODEFormer' is not supported across the board. Table 10 shows FIM-ODE is very weak in 3D (16.7% reconstruction, ~0% generalization on ID systems), and on the low-data benchmarks (Table 4) zero-shot FIM-ODE is substantially worse than classical baselines (e.g., 0.90 vs 0.03 for GP-DNF) and highly sensitive to the noise realisation (std of 7 on a mean of 0.8). The strong conclusions are drawn mostly from 1D/2D results.

The best finetuning results ('Finetuned 2') rely on checkpoint selection using the held-out evaluation window itself, which the authors concede is 'not a fully independent test protocol' (Appendix D.1). Since these finetuned numbers are the headline evidence that pretraining provides a useful initialization that 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines', this methodological weakness undercuts a central claim. The train-loss-selected variant (Finetuned 1) is far worse and highly variable.

Zero-shot transfer to real data is fragile: on two of three MoCap subjects FIM-ODE fails catastrophically zero-shot (MSE 655 and 295 in Table 5), and the paper itself admits the source of degradation is 'ambiguous'. This weakens the claimed broad applicability of the pretrained model.

The evaluation metric for ODEBench (fraction of systems with R^2 > 0.9) is a coarse binary threshold on only 59 systems; the advantage over ODEFormer largely disappears under the strict threshold for generalization (Table 2) and only reappears at a relaxed threshold (R^2 > 0.8), making the robustness claims dependent on threshold choice.

Some comparisons are asymmetric or indirect: FIM-ODE is restricted to the first three PCA components on MoCap while baselines use five, and ODEFormer is excluded from that experiment entirely, so the breadth of the evaluation is narrower than the framing suggests.

strengths: Clear and well-executed core idea: a simple polynomial prior (degree ≤ 3, dimensions 1–3) suffices to train a foundation inference model that matches or beats ODEFormer on ODEBench despite being ~10x smaller and pretrained on ~80x fewer systems, supporting the local-neural-operator vs. global-symbolic-representation argument.

Comprehensive and honest experimental treatment: failure cases are analyzed explicitly (the frictionless pendulum in Section 5.1, the poor zero-shot low-data results in Section 5.2), the test-set-based checkpoint selection for Finetuned 2 is disclosed in Appendix D.1, and the checkpoint-selection caveat is quantified (Table 6).

The interpretability contribution is genuine and well supported: querying the neural vector field for equilibria, Jacobians, and stability types (Figures 2, 13) exposes failure modes (e.g., the pendulum's conservative geometry) and qualitative wins (correct unstable-spiral classification on CDIMA where ODEFormer reverses stability) that trajectory error metrics alone would hide.

Good reproducibility posture: pretrained model, code, and tutorials are released; data generation, architecture, normalization, and finetuning hyperparameters are documented in detail across Appendices B–D, including runtime figures for finetuning (CPU-only, minutes-scale).

Ablations are thorough: context-size effects (Table 14), discretization and trajectory-count sweeps (Figures 14–19), dataset-size scaling (Figures 20–22), ID/OOD splits (Table 10), and degree-6 OOD generalization (Table 15).
Real-data validation on CMU MoCap with a clear-eyed analysis of where zero-shot fails and finetuning recovers performance (Section 5.3).
weaknesses: The abstract's claim of outperforming neural and GP baselines 'without requiring machine learning expertise' is not supported by the zero-shot evidence: in Table 4, zero-shot FIM-ODE (0.90/0.43/0.40) is far worse than GP-DNF (0.03/0.04/0.04); only after finetuning does it become competitive, and Finetuned 2 checkpoints are selected on the held-out evaluation window, which the authors themselves concede is not a fully independent test protocol. The strongest headline numbers thus rest on a compromised selection procedure.

The ODEBench evaluation is based on only ~59 systems, so differences of a few percentage points in Tables 1 and 2 carry high sampling uncertainty; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided. Some appendix cells (e.g., 3D ID generalization: 0.0% for FIM-ODE vs 5.6% for ODEFormer) actually favor the baseline.

Three-dimensional performance is markedly weak (Table 10: 16.7% reconstruction on 3D ID systems at zero corruption, 0% generalization), yet the abstract and introduction do not qualify that the strong zero-shot claim is largely driven by 1D and 2D systems; the flat aggregate numbers obscure this.

The 'large standard deviations' in Table 4 (e.g., 0.8(7), 2(1)) and the presentation of single-run FIM-ODE rows next to averaged rows make it hard to gauge the practical reliability of zero-shot inference in exactly the regimes the finetuning story is meant to address; Figure 12 additionally shows 'best-performing samples from 100 trials', which, while labeled, invites over-optimistic reading.

Novelty is modest: the architecture and training methodology are directly adapted from FIM-SDE (Seifner et al., 2025a), and the primary new elements are the prior design and the local-vs-global representation argument. The paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new beyond the prior and the ODE-specific identifiability discussion.

The generalization task on ODEBench (Table 2) is essentially a tie with ODEFormer (both around 27–33%), so the 'matching and often improving' claim holds mainly for reconstruction; the narrative in the abstract slightly overstates the breadth of the advantage.

Some design choices that materially affect the comparison (e.g., FIM-ODE's multi-trajectory conditioning versus ODEFormer's single-trajectory setting on ODEBench, and the effect of restricting the MoCap representation to three principal components) are discussed but not ablated in a way that fully isolates their contribution to the reported gains.
